context.objectives: Understand Banker's Algorithm and Coffman conditions for deadlock prevention.

examples.label: RELEVANT
examples.title: Banker's algorithm - Wikipedia
examples.text: The Banker's algorithm is a resource allocation and deadlock avoidance algorithm. It tests for safety by simulating the allocation of predetermined maximum possible amounts of all resources, and then makes an s-state check to test for possible deadlock conditions before deciding whether allocation should be allowed to continue. A system is in a safe state if there is a sequence of processes that can all complete.

examples.label: RELEVANT
examples.title: Deadlock prevention and the four Coffman conditions
examples.text: A deadlock can occur only if four Coffman conditions hold at the same time: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Deadlock prevention in an operating system works by ensuring that at least one of these conditions can never hold. For example, requiring processes to request all resources at once removes hold and wait.

examples.label: RELEVANT
examples.title: Detecting deadlock with a resource allocation graph
examples.text: Operating systems can detect deadlocks by building a resource allocation graph. A cycle in the graph means processes are waiting on each other for resources. Once a deadlock is detected, the system can recover by terminating a process or preempting resources from a blocked process.

examples.label: PARTIALLY_RELEVANT
examples.title: CPU scheduling algorithms in operating systems
examples.text: An operating system uses a scheduler to decide which process runs on the CPU next. Common algorithms include first come first served, shortest job first, round robin and priority scheduling. Each algorithm trades off throughput, waiting time and fairness. Context switching between processes has a cost that the scheduler must account for.

examples.label: PARTIALLY_RELEVANT
examples.title: Introduction to concurrency and threads
examples.text: Concurrent programs run several threads that share memory. Without synchronization, threads can corrupt shared data in a race condition. Mutexes and semaphores protect critical sections, but careless locking can make threads wait forever on each other, which programmers must avoid by acquiring locks in a consistent order.

context.objectives: Learn the light-dependent reactions and the Calvin cycle in plants.

examples.label: RELEVANT
examples.title: Light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis
examples.text: In the light-dependent reactions, chlorophyll in the thylakoid membrane absorbs light energy and splits water, releasing oxygen. The energy is used to make ATP and NADPH. These energy carriers then power the Calvin cycle in the stroma of the chloroplast, where carbon dioxide is fixed into sugar.

examples.label: RELEVANT
examples.title: The Calvin cycle explained
examples.text: The Calvin cycle uses ATP and NADPH from the light reactions to convert carbon dioxide into glucose. The enzyme RuBisCO fixes carbon dioxide onto ribulose bisphosphate. The cycle has three phases: carbon fixation, reduction, and regeneration of the starting molecule. Plants run this cycle in the stroma.

examples.label: PARTIALLY_RELEVANT
examples.title: Cellular respiration and the mitochondria
examples.text: Cells break down glucose to release energy in the form of ATP. Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm, while the citric acid cycle and the electron transport chain occur in the mitochondria. Plants and animals both rely on respiration, which uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.

examples.label: PARTIALLY_RELEVANT
examples.title: How to care for your houseplants
examples.text: Most houseplants need bright indirect sunlight and water only when the top inch of soil is dry. Overwatering is the most common mistake and can cause root rot. Feed your plants in spring and summer, and repot them when roots start growing out of the drainage holes.
